news.title: Jimmy Kimmel, James Talarico and the FCC’s Muzzling of the Media
news.text:
The ‘Campaign of Censorship and Control’

Will the Federal Communications Commission ever actually punish Disney or CBS for FCC Chairman Brendan Carr’s belief that those networks are in violation of the agency’s “equal time” rule?

We may never know the answer to that question, and that appears to be the point. 

Both networks have, in their own way, bowed to pressure from the Trump administration in muzzling themselves for the sake of avoiding something worse — or nothing! — from the sycophant running the FCC for Trump. And it’s not really either network’s fault. 

Comedian Jimmy Kimmel announced on Wednesday evening that his show chose to publish an interview that Kimmel conducted with Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico — who faces radioactive Republican candidate Ken Paxton in one of the most closely-watched Senate races of the 2026 midterms — on YouTube instead of attempting to air the discussion on his show, “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” The show is broadcast by Disney, which owns ABC, and has been engaged in an ongoing battle with the FCC as Carr attempts to use his post as head of the commission to bully the media into only broadcasting things President Trump likes.

The lawyers for the CBS-run show, “The Late Show With Stephen Colbert,” opted to do the same thing earlier this year after Carr announced that the FCC was investigating ABC’s daytime talkshow “The View” for airing an interview with the same Senate candidate. I get into this more in a piece here, but the rule that Carr is using to justify his threats and investigations was changed decades ago to extend exemptions to FCC’s “equal time” policy to talkshows, a bucket that The View, Colbert and Kimmel’s shows all fall under.

During his show on Wednesday evening, Kimmel explained his show’s decision, saying Trump and Carr had pressured ABC over “simple, traditional editorial decisions: guest bookings it would seem they don’t like.”

“Now that he’s president, his FCC has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations,” Kimmel continued. “So if you want to learn about a candidate for the Senate tomorrow, you will have to go to the ‘Jimmy Kimmel Live!’ YouTube channel.” 

You cannot blame the broadcaster, and I wouldn’t even call the move capitulation. Instead, it’s the manifestation of what Carr has sought to do with his post as FCC chair since Trump appointed him. It represents an effective chilling of press freedoms during a time when the federal government is using its might to shut down both dissent and stifle journalism that it does not like.

The sole Democrat on the Federal Communications Commission said as much in a statement on Thursday. 

“Jimmy Kimmel’s decision to keep his interview with a Senate candidate off the air shows just how far this Administration’s campaign of censorship and control has gone,” FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, who was appointed to the commission by President Biden, said. 

“There is no way to know how many other editorial decisions across the country have quietly been shaped by this same pressure,” Gomez continued. “No host, local affiliate, or network should have to weigh federal retaliation before booking a guest for a newsworthy interview. Any attempt to pressure broadcasters into self-censorship undermines both press freedom and the public’s right to hear from candidates in their communities seeking public office.”

GOPer Jumps to Write Trump Bribe Into Law

While reports surface suggesting that several Republican members of Congress were dismayed and caught off guard by President Trump’s speech last night — during which he bribed Americans into voting for Republicans in the midterms with the promise of $5,000 checks (read more from Hunter Walker last night here) — some are fine with Trump’s big bribe plan. That includes Vice President JD Vance, who went on Fox News today to try to sane-wash the suggestion that Trump could pay people for voting Republican. Essentially, he said there would be income bracket barriers to who can receive checks and the whole $1 trillion endeavor could be magically funded by tariff refunds 🤔

Then there’s Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-OH) from Ohio, vowing to get to work codifying Trump’s bribery scheme into federal law before the new Congress is sworn in. 

Dem Challenger Tests Political Saliency of Data Centers

Politico has a new report out today that looks at how the Democrat challenging Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA) is making the vulnerable Republican’s middle-ground approach to data center construction in Pennsylvania the focal point of his campaign. Fitzpatrick has been rather limp on the lightning-rod, bipartisan issue, as have most Republicans. He’s backed legislation that seeks to address rising electricity costs tied to data center development, and has said things like America “can innovate without compromising our communities.”

His Democratic challenger, on the other hand, has espoused beliefs more in line with most American voters who want the whole endeavor shut down. Per Politico: 

Democrat Bob Harvie’s first general-election ad in his campaign against Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick is calling for a data center moratorium, the latest sign artificial intelligence is emerging as a key midterm campaign issue.

“I’m Bob Harvie, I approve this message because I don’t want more data centers, I want a moratorium,” the Bucks County commissioner says in the 30-second ad. “Big Tech owns enough, they shouldn’t own our congressman, too.”

The race is one to watch because Fitzpatrick is viewed as a particularly vulnerable member of the House Republican conference. He’s a five-term congressman, but he’s one of three House Republicans who won a seat in a district that Kamala Harris won in the 2024 presidential election.

You’ll still get my newsletter delivered to your inbox every Monday-Thursday, and you will still be able to read the meatiest part of my column either in your email or on TPM’s website. A special note to my Substack readers: nothing will change for you, you’ll still get this sent to your inbox each evening, I just will be sending it out from TPM instead. 

If you love reading WTS every night and can’t imagine living without the whole thing, you should sign up to become a TPM member today ☺️ WTS readers are getting a special 50% off discount. Click here to join the TPM community! 

Read This From TPM Today

David Kurtz writes on the Justice Department making good on its threat to prosecute election officials nationwide who refuse to comply with the DOJ’s demand for access to states’ voter rolls, a demand that has been repeatedly shut down by federal judges across the country: 

What makes the escalation especially remarkable is that they come after the Justice Department has repeatedly struck out in civil lawsuits trying to force states to cough up voter information. Having lost in court while trying to clear the lower bar of a civil lawsuit, the Trump DOJ is now going to meet the even higher standard of a criminal prosecution?

news.title: Jeff Bezos’ Washington Post assures everyone talk of AI killing humans is nothing to fret about
news.text:
A Washington Post editorial invoked the Bible to downplay the potential threat posed by artificial intelligence and instead warned of looming government overreach against Big Tech — while failing to note that billionaire Post owner Jeff Bezos recently co-founded an AI company.

The unsigned editorial, published Wednesday evening under the headline “AI hysteria jumps the shark,” came in response to comments in which current and former Anthropic employees said people working on AI projects “earnestly believe” the technology could kill all humans within 10 years.

“Scripture warns against false prophets,” the Post's editors wrote. “The Gospel of Matthew says that no one but God, ‘not even the angels of heaven,’ knows the day or hour of the end times.”

The editorial, posted outside the news outlet’s formidable paywall, also condemned the “chilling sweep” of legislation proposed by independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Democratic Rep. Greg Casar of Texas to pause advanced AI development and ban “artificial superintelligence.”

“Politicians should not seek to regulate a fast-moving technology they don't understand,” the editors wrote.

The editorial made no mention of Amazon founder Bezos, who bought the Post for $250 million in 2013 and last month ranked No. 10 on Time's list of the most influential people in AI. 

The magazine cited his role as co-founder and co-CEO of the AI startup Prometheus, which was launched in November 2025 and valued at $41 billion in June, with Bezos telling CNBC that its work “will make it much easier for engineers to design physical objects.” 

A Post spokesperson didn't immediately respond to an inquiry from The Independent regarding the editorial's apparent lack of full disclosure.

The editorial came as Bezos — whose Blue Origin space company reportedly holds about $1.1 billion in federal contracts — has significantly softened his stance against President Donald Trump, with whom he feuded during Trump's first term over the Post's coverage of the White House.

Amazon, where Bezos is executive chairman and owns nearly nine percent of the company's stock, donated $1 million toward Trump's 2025 inauguration, which he attended with future wife Lauren Sánchez.

The company also gave an undisclosed amount to help fund construction of the president's controversial $600 million White House ballroom, and spent $40 million on a widely panned documentary about first lady Melania Trump that IMDb says grossed about $16.7 million worldwide.

The Post has also been undergoing a period of upheaval under Bezos, including the loss of about 300,000 subscribers and associate editor David Maraniss, a 48-year employee, after the owner vetoed a 2024 endorsement of Vice President Kamala Harris over Trump and ended the paper's practice of endorsing candidates.

The Post lost another 75,000 subscribers early last year after Bezos said its opinion pages would only promote “personal liberties and free markets,” leading to the resignation of top opinion editor David Shipley.

His right-leaning successor, Adam O'Neal, announced his resignation in July, telling colleagues it was best for him and his family, according to The New York Times. 

Several high-profile opinion columnists, including Pulitzer Prize winners Eugene Robinson and Jonathan Capehart, have also resigned or taken buyouts since the libertarian shift in the Post's editorial tone.

The spark for Wednesday's AI editorial was a series of Tuesday social media posts in which Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon said he'd resigned his position after three years “doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic.”

“Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” he wrote.

Coxon also said, “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

In response, Anthropic employee Evan Hubinger, who holds the title of alignment science lead, wrote, “Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!”

“I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” he added.

Spokespersons for Anthropic and OpenAI didn’t immediately respond to inquiries from The Independent.

The posts followed similar warnings about the potential impact of AI from major tech figures including Elon Musk, Google co-founder Eric Schmidt and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, a retired computer scientist who's been called the “godfather of AI.”

A 2024 survey of more than 4,000 AI researchers around the world found that only 3 percent “were most worried about the long-term, speculative scenario in which advanced, out-of-control AI poses a threat to human existence,” according to Responsible Ai UK, a group of British academics.

The most frequently cited concerns about AI were malicious use, misuse, misinformation and the impact on jobs, RAiUK said.

The Post's editorial came as polls have consistently shown that about seven in 10 Americans oppose AI-related data centers in their communities.

It acknowledged that predictions of people being killed by AI were “concerning” but said they “merit a certain skepticism.”

“People working at the frontier may know more than most about what today’s models can do. But that does not give them special knowledge of what machines that do not yet exist will someday become — or how society will adapt to the challenge,” it said.

The editorial also held out the promise of “the many potential upsides of AI, such as the developing breakthrough medicines.”

But left unsaid were the results of a May study, published by leading medical journal The Lancet, in which Columbia University researchers found that the rate of fabricated sources in biomedical papers surged 1,200 percent from 2023 to 2025, according to the University of Minnesota's Center for Infectious Disease Research & Policy. 

The authors offered several possible explanations, including intentional misconduct, but noted that previous studies found that up to 69% of AI-generated references in “biomedical contexts” were made up.
news.summary: The news outlet, whose owner recently co-founded an AI company, instead warned about looming government overreach against Big Tech

news.title: At the Races: Defiant in Dallas
news.text:
Welcome to At the Races! Each week we bring you news and analysis from the CQ Roll Call campaign team. Know someone who’d like to get this newsletter? They can subscribe here.

By Daniela Altimari, Mary Ellen McIntire and Niels Lesniewski

DALLAS – Recent national polls show President Donald Trump’s job approval rating sinking to historic lows, driven by deep dissatisfaction over rising prices, including gas topping $4 a gallon, fueled by an unpopular conflict with Iran and his tariffs policy.

But if any of that has the Republican faithful feeling down about the party’s prospects in the midterm elections, they aren’t saying.

“I feel good about our candidates,’’ said Scott Martin, a state senator from Lancaster, Pa., in town for this week’s Republican mini-convention. 

“And obviously, Pennsylvania is not only just critically important for presidential elections,’’ he added. “It’s also critically important to where the numbers end up in the U.S. Congress.”

Admittedly, the target audience for the two-day gathering isn’t politically independent voters who will decide key races in purple districts: Many of those voters have soured on Trump and might be tuning out the “Trumpapalooza convention” — which might explain why some swing district Republican candidates opted to skip the trip to Dallas altogether.

Instead, the emphasis here was on firing up MAGA voters who tend to sit out elections when Trump isn’t on the ballot.

“This historic midterm convention is rallying Republicans at the perfect time because so much is on the line this November,’’ House Majority Leader Steve Scalise told the crowd at the American Airlines Center. “President Trump’s America First agenda is at stake.”

The party in the White House typically loses seats in a midterm election, and Trump acknowledged Wednesday that history is not on his side. That might explain the scattershot approach his nearly two-hour keynote speech took, from painting Democratic candidates as dangerous and “crazed lunatics” and communists whose agenda would jeopardize the American way of life to his audacious pledge to pay every American $5,000 if the GOP holds the House and the Senate this fall.

But above all, he staked the election on his own personal appeal. 

“A president, Democrat or Republican, almost never wins the midterms,’’ he told the audience. “We've got to change that because we have something going that's so good. We can't let that string be broken.”

“So I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot.”

Starting gate

More from Dallas: Day One of Republicans’ midterm spectacular saw a stream of lawmakers and candidates taking the stage at the American Airlines Center, and Roll Call photo editor Bill Clark was there to capture the best moments. And our colleague John T. Bennett runs down how Trump tried to tether himself to his party’s quest to retain its majorities in Congress. 

#NHSEN: New Hampshire’s Senate matchup between Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas and Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu is set after both handily won their respective primaries Tuesday. Further down the ballot, Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, won the Democratic nomination for Pappas’ 1st District seat, emerging from a bitter primary fight against Maura Sullivan.

Missouri’s mess, resolved? The Supreme Court appeared to confirm Thursday that Missouri will use a congressional map approved in 2022 for this year’s midterm elections, our colleague Michael Macagnone reports. The justices paused an order from a federal trial court judge that had directed the state to use a map the Republican-led legislature passed last year. Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver II, whose district was targeted by Republicans, should face an easier path to reelection under the 2022 map, a boost for Democrats in the fight for the House. 

New targets: The NRCC added five candidates to its “MAGA Majority” program for strong challengers, including four running in Florida districts that were redrawn to favor the GOP. The additions come after the committee dropped New York state Sen. Peter Oberacker, who is challenging freshman Democrat Josh Riley in the 19th District, from the program. 

25 years later: A quarter century after the 9/11 attacks, advocates for contingency plans on Capitol Hill in case of a mass-casualty catastrophe say lawmakers haven’t done enough to ensure continuity of Congress, Roll Call’s Nina Heller reports. 

Census changes: The Trump administration proposed a rule to exclude undocumented and temporary immigrants from the data used to determine the number of congressional seats allotted to each state after the 2030 census, Macagnone writes. The effort, an extension of a push from Trump’s first term, is likely to draw legal challenges and fights in Congress over its implementation.

#RIGOV: Helena Foulkes, a former CVS executive, defeated Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee in Wednesday’s Democratic gubernatorial primary, making McKee the first sitting governor to lose a primary since Kansas’ Jeff Colyer in 2018. Rhode Island Sen. Jack Reed, meanwhile, easily beat two primary opponents as the Democrat seeks a sixth term.

Staying put: Democratic Sen. John Fetterman, already estranged from some members of his party, made headlines Wednesday for a video message he recorded to introduce his fellow Pennsylvanian, Republican Sen. Dave McCormick, at the GOP midterm convention. But Fetterman insisted in a statement that he remained a “lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly with my party — and should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on.”

Ad watch: Virginia prosecutor Shannon Taylor, who’s challenging GOP Rep. Rob Wittman, released an ad touting her role in prosecuting a state senator who served jail time for his relationship with a teenage girl. “I didn’t care that he was a Democrat or the pressure that I got to make it go away," she says in the spot. In Pennsylvania’s 7th District, Democrat Bob Brooks, a retired firefighter taking on Republican freshman Ryan Mackenzie, launched his first general election ad, which features a literal dumpster fire. “I’ll cut off the fuel. Smoke out the billionaires and their lobbyists,” Brooks says on camera. Meanwhile, a super PAC supporting Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s Senate race released an ad tied to the 25th anniversary of 9/11 that includes footage of the attack and progressive streamer Hasan Piker saying that “America deserved 9/11” – a remark he later walked back. Rogers, a former House Intelligence chairman, faces Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who campaigned with Piker during the primary.

Rebuffing Buffett: Brinker Harding, the Republican nominee in Nebraska’s “blue dot” 2nd District, is running a campaign ad that features the “Oracle of Omaha,’’ investor and philanthropist Warren Buffett, despite a request from Buffett’s family to take it down. “It implies that my dad endorses him. He did not have permission to use it," Buffett’s daughter, Susie Buffett, told KETV in Omaha. Harding faces Democrat Denise Powell in the race to succeed retiring GOP Rep. Don Bacon. 

There’s always tweets: Democrat Will Lawrence, who is challenging GOP Rep. Tom Barrett in Michigan’s battleground 7th District, is the latest candidate whose past social media posts earned a review by CNN’s KFILE. Lawrence’s deleted posts included embraces of the "defund the police” movement and abolishing prisons and attacks on the nuclear family home.

Democratic endorsements: The Congressional Black Caucus PAC has endorsed Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat running for Michigan’s open Senate seat. The group backed Rep. Haley Stevens during the Democratic primary. In Texas, Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico picked up the backing of nearly two dozen current and former Republican officials, including former Dallas Mayor Steve Bartlett and former Texas Supreme Court Chief Justice Tom Phillips. And in Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton won the support of Republican former Gov. Bill Graves in his challenge to GOP Sen. Roger Marshall. 

Not in Dallas: Former congressional aide Sydney Gruters, the Republican nominee for Florida’s 16th District and wife of RNC Chairman Joe Gruters, is among the House GOP candidates who didn’t travel to Dallas for the party’s midterm convention. Gruters faces Democrat Kelly Kirschner, a former Sarasota mayor, in the race to succeed retiring Republican Rep. Vern Buchanan.

Nathan’s notes

Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales announced more race rating changes last week, 10 in Democrats’ direction. The lone race that moved Republicans’ way was New Hampshire’s Senate contest, which is now rated a Toss-up. 

Contests once seen as solid for the GOP that moved to “Likely Republican” include the Senate race in Kansas and Florida’s gubernatorial election. 

“For now, the battleground continues to shift incrementally toward Democrats as we wait to see if Republicans will bounce back or if the bottom falls out from under them and an unpopular president in the White House,” Nathan writes.

What we’re reading

MAGA’s millions: The pro-Trump MAGA, Inc. super PAC has begun doling out its $400 million war chest in six battleground Senate races and one competitive House race, The New York Times reports. The spending comes via a new group, No Going Back PAC Inc., which, with $49 million in reservations early this week, quickly became one of the cycle’s top spenders. 

Tit for tat: The Washington Post reports that the trade war with Canada, which escalated this week, could have outsize effects in midterm battleground states such as Michigan, Pennsylvania and Maine, where tariffs on some steel and iron products and on logging equipment could spike costs. 

Tennessee appointment: Axios Nashville looks at the sweepstakes for the Senate seat currently held by Republican Marsha Blackburn, who would be able to appoint her successor should she prevail, as expected, in the governor’s race in November.

#MESEN: The newly renamed Washington Sun reports on the high-stakes Senate race in Maine, where GOP Sen. Susan Collins is trying to overcome the Trump administration’s ICE and trade policies as Democrat Troy Jackson is essentially running a 100-day race seeking to capitalize on frustrations with Collins. The incumbent called it “the strangest race I’ve ever seen.”

The count: 15 percent

That's how many registered voters say they plan to return their ballots by mail or drop them off at the post office this year, according to the latest Economist/YouGov poll.

Those plans could be complicated by the Trump administration’s push, in coordination with the U.S. Postal Service, to institute new rules that would make voting by mail dramatically more difficult. Two dozen states have objected to the rules on both constitutional and logistical grounds, and have argued in court that the changes would be impossible to implement, with the process already underway.

Already this week – days after the administration petitioned the Supreme Court to intervene and allow the currently blocked rules to take effect – state election officials have begun taking actions ranging from sending out ballots early to considering how to cut the USPS out of their process.

While Trump often votes by mail himself, he has consistently attacked the process, which he feels advantages Democrats.

Conservative elections lawyer Ben Ginsburg said recently that Republicans could be hurt by the restrictions, though the Economist/YouGov poll found that just 10 percent of Trump 2024 voters were planning to cast their ballots by mail. More than 20 percent of Kamala Harris voters said the same.

–by Roll Call’s Ryan Kelly

Key race: #IA02

Candidates: Republican Sen. Joni Ernst’s retirement sparked a political chain reaction in the Hawkeye State. Rep. Ashley Hinson is running for Senate, leaving behind the open 2nd District. Vying to succeed her are Republican Joe Mitchell, a former state representative and housing developer who launched Run Gen Z, which encourages young conservatives to run for office; and Presbyterian minister and Democratic state Rep. Lindsay James.

Why it matters; Democrats are increasingly bullish on Iowa, a onetime swing state that has become solidly Republican in the Trump era. Trump’s policies on tariffs and the ongoing conflict in Iran have spiked costs overall, and farmers, who rely on diesel fuel and fertilizer, have been hard hit. Last month, Inside Elections shifted the race rating from Likely Republican to Lean Republican.

Cash dash: James reported raising $1.6 million through June 30, while Mitchell brought in $1.9 million, including a $100,000 candidate loan, over that same period.

Backers: Mitchell, who considered Charlie Kirk as a mentor, has the backing of Turning Point Action, the organization Kirk founded. He also has Trump’s endorsement, although The Washington Post reported that he recently toned down references to the president on his campaign website. The DCCC has included James on its “Red to Blue” list, which provides extra resources and support to top recruits. She also has the backing of EMILY’s List and gun safety groups Giffords PAC and Everytown for Gun Safety.

What they’re saying: James has highlighted cost of living concerns, asserting that elected officials have a “moral obligation“ to address systemic injustices. Mitchell has called for new ethical standards for members of Congress. He touts an anti-corruption message that includes term limits, a ban on insider trading and prohibiting campaigns from taking contributions from corporate PACs, the Iowa Capital Dispatch reported.

Terrain: The district covers the state’s northeastern corner, bordering Wisconsin and Minnesota, and includes the cities of Cedar Rapids and Dubuque. Trump carried the district by 10 points in 2024. 

Wild card: Top-of-the-ticket dynamics. Iowa Democrats are hopeful that a strong showing by their nominees for governor, state Auditor Rob Sand, and for Ernst’s open Senate seat, state Rep. Josh Turek, will boost Democratic candidates down ballot, including James and other House hopefuls.

The House and Senate are scheduled to return to Washington on Monday. A day later, the regular primary season officially wraps up, with intraparty elections in Delaware. But Louisiana will be holding all-party jungle primaries for their House seats on Nov. 3 as a consequence of redistricting earlier this year.

Photo finish

Georgia Rep. Mike Collins, who is challenging Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, speaks during the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

news.title: Cooper vs. Whatley—What North Carolina Polls Show Under 2 Months to Midterm
news.text: Former Democratic North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper holds a double-digit lead over Republican Michael Whatley in a new poll released less than two months before Election Day in a race that could help determine which party controls the Senate. A new Elon University poll of 800 voters released Thursday found Cooper holding an 11-point lead over Whatley—49 percent to 38 percent—among likely voters, while posting an even wider margin among registered voters. The poll comes as Democrats eye a narrow path to reclaiming control of the upper chamber, where Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority. Polling suggests that the North Carolina Senate race is one of the Democrats' top flip opportunities in the midterms. To take back the majority, Democrats must defend their current seats—including in two states President Donald Trump won in his 2024 White House bid—and flip four others. North Carolina has long been a closely watched battleground state despite last electing a Democratic Senator in 2008. Trump has won the state three times, carrying it by about 1.3 percentage points over Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 and increasing that margin to roughly 3.2 points against Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024. Despite backing the GOP in 11 of the last 12 presidential elections, Democrats have had success at the statewide level, winning 8 of the last 9 governor races in the Tarheel State. Jeff Allen, Cooper for North Carolina campaign manager, told Newsweek in a Thursday email, “Roy Cooper has spent his career putting North Carolinians first, while Washington DC insider Michael Whatley spent his delivering for billionaires and special interests at the expense of the middle class.” The statement continued, “A Democrat has not won statewide federal office in North Carolina in nearly two decades and we know this race will be very close, which is why we’re building a campaign to earn every vote and make sure North Carolinians know that Roy Cooper will fight for them in the Senate." Newsweek has reached out to Whatley’s press team for comment via email on Thursday. North Carolina Senate Race The North Carolina Senate race is for the seat currently held by Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who is not seeking reelection. Cooper, who served as North Carolina governor from 2017 through 2024, is seeking a return to elected office. Whatley is the former chairman of the Republican National Committee (RNC) and the North Carolina Republican Party. The race is widely viewed as one of Democrats' best pickup opportunities in 2026 and is expected to play a key role in the battle for Senate control. North Carolina Senate Race: Latest Poll Among likely voters in the Elon poll, Cooper leads Whatley 49 percent to 38 percent, with 8 percent undecided. Among registered voters, Cooper's support remains unchanged at 49 percent, while Whatley's slips to 36 percent, widening the gap slightly, with 14 percent undecided or backing someone else. The findings point to a major name-recognition advantage for Cooper. Nearly three-quarters of registered voters, 71 percent, said they had heard "a great deal" or "some" about the former governor, compared with 47 percent for Whatley. Just 4 percent said they had never heard of Cooper, while 15 percent said they had never heard of Whatley. Christopher Cooper, a political science professor at Western Carolina University, told Newsweek that the poll is “just the latest showing Roy Cooper ahead,” adding that “the basic storylines—that Cooper leads Whatley and that Whatley has a name recognition problem--is undoubtedly true at this stage.” He added that the real “question is whether this series of poor polling results for Whatley results in the GOP reducing spending in North Carolina.” Cooper has a substantial fundraising advantage in the race. Federal Elections Commission (FEC) finance filings show the Democrat had about $20.7 million cash on hand at the end of June, compared with roughly $3.4 million for Whatley. Economic concerns remain the dominant issue for North Carolina voters heading into the election. The poll found that 86 percent of registered voters rated inflation and the cost of living as "very important" factors in their voting decisions, while 73 percent said the same about the economy and health care. North Carolina voters appeared generally wary of U.S. military involvement in Iran. A majority, 52 percent, opposed the intervention, while 31 percent supported it. The poll was conducted from August 21 to August 31 and has a margin of error of plus or minus 5.6 percentage points for likely voters and 5.05 percentage points for registered voters. “Despite an increase in advertising, we measured relatively little movement over the last month in voter intentions about the U.S. Senate race in North Carolina, with Democratic candidate Roy Cooper maintaining a strong lead over Republican Michael Whatley,” Jason Husser, director of the Elon University Poll and professor of political science and public policy said in the poll’s release. What Other Polls Show Other recent polls have shown Cooper with a notable lead over Whatley. A High Point University poll found Cooper leading Whatley 50 percent to 45 percent, a 5-point advantage that falls within the poll’s 5.2-percentage-point credibility interval. The poll shows that 3 percent are unsure or would not vote and 3 percent would pick someone else or another party. The survey of 800 self-identified registered voters, including 660 likely voters, was conducted August 3 to August 12. A poll from the Carolina Journal showed Cooper ahead of Whatley by 12.5 points, 51.5 percent to 39 percent. Other candidates received support from 4.7 percent of respondents, while 4.8 percent were still undecided. The poll surveyed 600 respondents from August 9 to August 10, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. An Elon University poll showed Cooper up 11 points, 53 percent to 42 percent. Three percent of respondents said they would vote for other candidates, while 2 percent were still undecided. Cooper’s lead was bolstered by his support among independents, who broke for him 49 percent to Whatley’s 22 percent, according to the poll. It surveyed 800 North Carolina voters from July 23 to July 31, 2026, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 5.6 percentage points. A Fox News poll showed Cooper up 9 points, 53 percent to 44 percent. It surveyed 1,005 registered voters from July 23 to July 27. It was conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. The Cook Political Report rates the race as Lean Democratic, writing in an April update, “We’ve long believed the North Carolina Senate race is the GOP seat Democrats are most likely to flip.” Sabato’s Crystal Ball shares the same rating. Nate Silver’s Silver Bulletin aggregate puts Cooper with an 8.5 point lead, 51.8 percent to Whatley's 43.2 percent. Prediction markets also point to a strong advantage for Cooper. As of Thursday, both Kalshi and Polymarket gave the former governor better than a 90 percent chance of defeating Whatley in the North Carolina Senate race. With early in-person voting set to begin in five weeks, on October 15, the race is entering a critical stretch. Democrats' Chances of Flipping the Senate Democrats need to flip four Republican-held seats and hold all of their own to take control of the chamber, which Republicans currently control 53-47. Historically, the party in the White House loses seats in the midterms and Democrats have been optimistic about their chances of winning a majority in both chambers. Nate Silver’s Silver Bulletin’s averages show Democrats leading in exactly four GOP-held Senate races, putting the party within reach of the four seats it needs, but with little room for error. Its latest updated averages shows Democrats ahead in North Carolina, Georgia, Minnesota, Maine, Ohio, New Hampshire, Michigan, Texas and Alaska. Republicans lead in Iowa, Kansas and Florida. The most competitive races in seats Democrats currently hold are in Georgia and Michigan, both of which narrowly backed Trump in the 2024 presidential election but did back former President Joe Biden in 2020. Democrats view GOP-held seats in Maine, which backed former Vice President Kamala Harris by 7 points, and North Carolina, which backed Trump by 3 points, as their top flip opportunities. Prediction markets remain divided on which party will control the Senate after the midterms. As of Thursday, Kalshi gave Republicans a 52 percent chance of winning control of the chamber, while Polymarket slightly favored Democrats, giving them a 53 percent chance of securing a Senate majority. Discussing North Carolina's importance to Democrats' Senate hopes, Robert Y. Shapiro, a political science professor at Columbia University, previously told Newsweek that the race is "a must-win seat in the Senate for the Democrats if they are to have any chance of controlling the Senate." Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Geoffrey Rowland.
news.summary: A new poll shows Roy Cooper leading Michael Whatley by double digits in North Carolina's closely watched Senate race.

news.title: How Jeff Bezos’s Space Race Against Elon Musk Made Him Cozy Up to Trump
news.text:
As a teenager he attended a NASA high school program in Huntsville, Alabama, the town known as Space City. The book that most influenced him was Gerard K. O’Neill’s The High Frontier: Human Colonies in Space (1976). O’Neill, a physics professor at Princeton, argued for the practical possibility of building human habitats that would float between Earth and the moon, housing tens of thousands of people in hermetic environments with earthlike gravity and climate.
At Princeton, he told classmates he wanted to build a company capable of colonizing space. He sat in on O’Neill’s seminars and led the campus chapter of Students for the Exploration and Development of Space. Bezos soon concluded that he would never be a top‑tier theoretical physicist. His road to space would have to run through business.
In 2000, Bezos founded his space company, Blue Origin. At first it was closer to a hobby than a business. In early Seattle days he launched homemade rockets in a public park alongside the sci‑fi writer Neal Stephenson, whom he hired as the company’s first employee. If Amazon took seven years to turn a profit, Blue Origin might never do so. Bezos would begin building the infrastructure needed to boldly go where no man had gone before through methodical, incremental improvement—customer obsession applied to space. The program to send tourists on short suborbital flights aboard the reusable New Shepard rocket moved slowly, with the loss of unmanned test vehicles in 2011 and 2015 before the company finally achieved a successful landing.
Elon Musk, meanwhile, threw himself into SpaceX, employing ten times as many people and eventually generating billions in revenue. He skipped the nine‑minute tourist hops to sixty thousand feet. Instead, he lofted actual commercial and military satellites into orbit with his Falcon 9 rocket and won NASA’s contract to resupply the International Space Station.
The contrast between the two men was stark. Bezos wasn’t visibly damaged by his childhood. He hadn’t built a reputation as a superlative engineer or technical inventor. He wasn’t a manic exhibitionist. Rational risk‑taking defined his career. He had one romantic partner and a reasonable number of children with normal names. Where Musk flaunted his personal chaos, Bezos hid his private life with monkish discipline.
Their motivations for going to space diverged just as sharply. If Silicon Valley’s spiritual poles are Mr. Spock and Ayn Rand, Bezos was always Team Star Trek. Optimism, love of exploration, and a dedication to problem‑solving shaped his belief that Blue Origin’s mission was expanding humanity’s potential.
Musk’s vision was darker, more Fountainhead than Federation. In-stead of revisiting the moon, he wanted to build a self‑sustaining city on Mars—Plan B for a species likely to destroy Earth through nuclear war or runaway AI.
Both men faced the same engineering and economic challenges: How do you land and reuse rockets? How do you make space a sustainable business—tourism, satellite launches, or government projects? On these fronts, SpaceX vastly outperformed Blue Origin. While Musk went hard after NASA and Pentagon contracts, Bezos didn’t pursue government work until 2010, and not seriously until 2018.
In 2015, Bezos decided to get serious. After finally pulling off a suborbital launch and landing, he announced in 2017 that he would sell $1 billion in Amazon stock annually to fund expansion. He began spending one day a week at Blue Origin and launched a search for its first real CEO. He accelerated work on New Glenn, Blue Origin’s first orbital‑class rocket, designed to compete with Musk’s Falcon 9, and began going after contracts to launch satellites.
This new focus coincided with a broader midlife reinvention. In 2017, at fifty‑three, Bezos stepped back from daily responsibilities at Amazon. That year he overtook Bill Gates as the world’s richest man, thanks to Amazon’s soaring stock price, Gates’s extensive philanthropy, and Bezos’s lack of philanthropy. Bezos also transformed himself physically, shedding his fleece‑and‑khakis persona and emerging as a gym-sculpted, bullet‑headed replica of Picard. “I am not the kind of person women fall in love with,” he once told Playboy. “I sort of grow on them, like a fungus.” As the Bezos muscles bulged, space beckoned. “I get increasing conviction with every passing year that Blue Origin, the space company, is the most important work I’m doing,” he said onstage at an event in May 2018.
That can’t have been music to many ears at The Washington Post.
In August 2013, the Graham family announced that its company was selling the paper to Bezos for $250 million in cash. The Grahams were beloved proprietors, but the Post had been losing money for years, and Donald Graham no longer saw a plausible path to sustainability. Bezos brought exactly what the paper lacked—a long time horizon and the capital to experiment without panic. Graham was explicit with Bezos that the Post could not become his political instrument and Bezos accepted those terms. He kept the widely respected Marty Baron in place as editor and told the staff he would protect the Post’s values while investing in the product and in technology.
For years, he did that. But why Bezos wanted the Post was never entirely clear. People close to him offered a blend of motives. The Post was a hard problem to solve and Bezos liked difficult business puzzles. It also gave him the opportunity to be a different kind of public figure, a steward of a democratic institution rather than simply the architect of an online empire. And $250 million for a national newspaper of record was a bargain.
Trump, of course, viewed news ownership as simply a lever of power. To him, every outlet was either for him or against him—and the Post was clearly against him. In May 2016, the presumptive Republican nominee launched into a tirade against Bezos on Hannity. “He bought this paper for practically nothing,” Trump said, “and he’s using that as a tool for political power against me . . . we can’t let him get away with it.” Bezos, he insisted, was using the Post “for political purposes, to save Amazon in terms of taxes and in terms of antitrust.” Trump referred to the paper as “the Amazon Washington Post,” as though it were all just Bezos Inc.
Bezos responded with measured firmness. Trump’s threats were “not an appropriate way for a presidential candidate to behave,” he told Baron in a public interview. Throughout the first term, Bezos remained an admirable if inscrutable owner.
The newsroom rewarded his restraint. It broke the news about Trump’s Access Hollywood tape and continued reporting aggressively, exposing lie upon lie, grift upon grift. Bezos never tried to alter coverage, even when it came at a cost to Amazon. He followed the example of the Post’s legendary publisher Katharine Graham, who stood up to pressure from the Nixon administration through both the Pentagon Papers showdown and Watergate.
Trump didn’t succeed in punishing Bezos on postal rates, taxes, or antitrust. Where he was able to hurt him was on Amazon’s bid to build JEDI, the Joint Enterprise Defense Infrastructure, a winner-take‑all $10 billion contract to move all of the Defense Department’s data to a centralized cloud. The program was supposed to allow the Pentagon to communicate more effectively with battlefields and to make greater use of AI. In July 2019, Trump said he might intervene in the decision. A few months later, the award went to Microsoft Azure over Amazon Web Services, which was widely seen as the market leader in cloud computing and the technical favorite.
People joked that buying the Post hadn’t cost Bezos $250 million—it had cost him $10.25 billion.
In early 2019, the midlife reinvention that had made Bezos so visibly swole collided with tabloid politics. On January 9, he and MacKenzie announced their divorce after twenty‑five years of marriage—hours before the National Enquirer published details of Bezos’s relationship with Lauren Sánchez.
The divorce that followed was orderly and unusually civil by plutocrat standards. In April 2019, MacKenzie Scott received 25 percent of the couple’s Amazon shares (and granted Jeff voting control over them). She took no stake in Blue Origin or the Post. She promptly committed herself to large‑scale philanthropy, pledging to give all of her money away.
Jeff wanted to spend more of his. He commissioned a 417‑foot sailing yacht that would be the largest in the world. He called it the Koru, a Māori term for an uncoiling fern, with the symbolic meaning of new life and growth. The ship’s figurehead, a voluptuous goddess with feathery wings, appeared to depict a blend of a Norse deity and his pneumatic fiancée.
While Bezos was remaking his personal life, Elon Musk was opportunistically aligning himself with power. In May 2024, Musk met with Trump in Palm Beach and reportedly discussed an advisory role in his future administration. Then, minutes after a would‑be assassin’s bullet grazed Trump’s ear at a Pennsylvania rally, Musk endorsed him outright and began donating immense sums to his campaign.
After Trump won the election, Musk—now in the catbird seat—moved to protect his position by advising Trump that Bezos was not his friend.
Bezos started ingratiating himself with the most accessible Trumps first: Ivanka and Jared. He and Lauren Sánchez were their neighbors in the gated island community of Indian Creek, the so‑called “Billionaire Bunker” adjacent to Miami Beach. After the July 13 assassination attempt, Bezos proffered praise for Trump’s “courage.”
Bezos’s big intervention was canceling The Washington Post’s planned endorsement of Kamala Harris. Bezos said he had grown concerned that endorsements created “a perception of bias.” Editorial page editor David Shipley couldn’t dissuade him. On X, Marty Baron called the decision “cowardice, with democracy as its casualty,” adding that Trump would treat it as “an invitation to further intimidate” Bezos. At the very least, it meant an invitation to dinner at Mar‑a‑Lago, where Melania pitched her documentary and Musk joined the table later in the evening. Musk’s announcement on X that “it was a great conversation” sealed the reset. The man who couldn’t be blackmailed, could, it now seemed, be blackmailed.
Trump embraced the restart and invited Bezos to his inauguration, requiring only a $1 million contribution from Amazon. Bezos, in a blue suit, and Sánchez, in a white pantsuit with a plunging neckline and bustier, stood prominently among the billionaire donors behind Trump at the ceremony.
Soon afterward, Bezos announced a new editorial philosophy for the Post’s opinion section. It would “write every day in support and defense of two pillars: personal liberties and free markets.” Trump, unsurprisingly, was delighted. “I’ve gotten to know him, and I think he’s trying to do a real job,” he told Fox News in March 2025. “Jeff Bezos is trying to do a real job with The Washington Post, and that wasn’t happening before.”
As of this writing, there have been no credible reports of Bezos interfering in news coverage. But his capitulation on the editorial page cast a long shadow over the newsroom and prompted an exodus of top political and investigative reporters. In February 2026, the paper laid off about 30 percent of its staff, reducing the newsroom by more than three hundred people.
Meanwhile, Blue Origin was back in contention for government contracts -- and now potentially to be favored over SpaceX. In June 2025, Trump threatened to cancel all of Musk’s government contracts. Musk exploded. On X, he threatened to cut off SpaceX’s shuttle service to the International Space Station, the only way NASA had to ferry astronauts. NASA, the Pentagon, and other agencies began calling Blue Origin, to ask whether they could fill the gap. In the new privatized space race, fealty and favoritism would drive outcomes, as they did with everything else under Trump.
Amazon found itself in a better place as well. When news leaked that the company was considering displaying tariff costs at checkout, Trump called Bezos. Whether the plan ever truly existed is unclear, but the possibility disappeared overnight. Bezos, who saw his self- interest as synonymous with the extra- planetary future of humanity, needed to keep the president happy.
“Jeff Bezos is very nice. He was terrific, he solved a problem very quickly,” Trump said after the call. “He did the right thing. He’s a good guy.”
Bezos did not respond or cooperate with Weisberg for Profiles in Cowardice.

news.summary: In an exclusive excerpt from Profiles in Cowardice: A Study of Collaboration in the Trump Era, Jacob Weisberg paints a revealing portrait of Bezos, from a science-fiction-loving schoolboy with dreams of being an astronaut to a billionaire hell-bent on getting what he wants.

news.title: Elon Musk Threatens to Sue Over Explosive New Documentary as Lawyer Claims Alex Gibney's Film Is Biased
news.text:
Elon Musk has responded to the implication that he influenced the 2024 election, RadarOnline.com has learned.

The world's richest man hit documentarian Alex Gibney with a cease-and-desist after the film Musk debuted at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival on Tuesday, September 8.Elon Musk Threatens LawsuitMusk's high-profile attorney, Alex Spiro, put Gibney and his team "on notice" before the film's full theatrical release on October 16, claiming "the insinuation is false."

Spiro zeroed in on a claim made by Musk's ex, Ashley St. Clair, who claimed, "He had told me (before the election) he was going to unleash the 'anomaly in the matrix.'"

The film thus suggested Musk was planning to alter the vote counts during the 2024 election between President Donald Trump and former Vice President Kamala Harris in favor of the Republican candidate. St. Clair claimed Musk told her, "I have ten thousand lasers in space."

She implied those lasers might be linked to Musk's telecommunications company Starlink. "I mean, I don't know where else he has space lasers," she says in the documentary.

However, according to Spiro, the insinuation is false, telling the producers that the contrary information "is public." Spiro claimed the creators of the film "chose not to be told the rest."Documentarian Allegedly 'Declined to Hear' Other SideIn the letter, obtained by The New York Post, he added, "Starlink was not connected to vote tabulation. Election officials in multiple states, independent cybersecurity researchers, and fact-checkers publicly refuted the Starlink vote-rigging claim in November 2024, and nothing since has revived it."

According to the attorney, Musk's team previously offered additional information to the production team, but they allegedly "declined to hear." Spiro claimed the satellites in space "communicate by laser inter-satellite link." 

Spiro directly called out the filmmaker, saying, "Mr. Gibney’s method is avowedly not neutral. Accepting a career achievement award in 2013, he described objectivity as a ‘folly,’ urged that every filmmaker should hold a point of view, and explained that he gravitates toward abuses of power precisely because of his own belief that powerful people lie more readily than anyone else."Alex Gibney Hits BackGibney reacted to the lawsuit threat and said, "Musk claims to be a 'free speech absolutist.' It appears that he is more interested in FEE speech."

Musk previously took a personal bite at Gibney after calling the film a "hit piece" in 2023, just as the film's production was beginning. With the movie not yet fully fleshed out, Gibney replied on X, "How would you know?"

However, Musk doubled down on his hit piece claim, alleging the filmmaker has "zero integrity" and creates "boring" movies. He added on September 10, "Gibney deliberately set out to make a hit piece and lacks any integrity whatsoever."Elon Musk Denies Ashley St. Clair NDA ClaimThe latest legal battle comes after Musk publicly disputed a different claim from his ex. St. Clair claimed she rejected a $40million non-disclosure agreement from Musk. He hasn't yet indicated if he plans to challenge St. Clair in court over the claim.

Explaining why she allegedly opted to avoid taking the money, she said at the Venice event, "I want to set the example for my kids that you should never take being materially comfortable over speaking the truth."

Musk denied the claim, writing, "She was never offered that and has a history of making false claims."
news.summary: 'Musk,' a film that explores Elon Musk's life, caused the billionaire to send a cease-and-desist to the filmmaker.

news.title: Donald Trump Claims America 'Wouldn't Even Exist' Today if Kamala Harris Had Beaten Him in 2024 Election
news.text:
Donald Trump has suggested that the U.S. would not exist today if Kamala Harris had been elected president in 2024, RadarOnline.com can report.

The president took the podium at night one of the GOP's new midterm convention, trying to convince voters to keep Republicans in control of Congress – by offering money for their votes.Trump Touts Himself at 'Trumpapalooza'Trump kicked off the midterm convention, which was modeled after the more traditional conventions held by each political party during election years. 

The 80-year-old delivered the keynote address on Wednesday night in Dallas at what has been billed by some as "Trumpapalooza."

Meanwhile, the president's overall approval rating continues to crater at unprecedented levels, and Republican strategists are worried they could end up losing one, if not both, houses of Congress. 

But don't tell that to Trump, who took a premature victory lap addressing supporters, and boasted that before he took office a second time, the country was in a tailspin.

"We were going down the drain. If we hadn't won the last election, I'm not sure that our country right now would even exist," Trump said. "It was going so bad."'Complete Failure of a President'However, Trump critics begged to differ online. 

"We've alienated every ally, demonstrated to the world that Americans can't be trusted by electing Trump, destroyed our education and health systems, and turned the White House into an unprecedented grift machine," one person countered. 

Another user blasted, "Complete failure of a president, complete failure of a political party. The rats should be fleeing the sinking ship at this point."

While one commentator targeted Trump's fan base: "MAGA shouldn't even exist in this country, much less inexplicably survive all of the arrows it takes on the daily for its dumb leader and his dumb lies... and yet here we are."Voters Poised to Ride a Blue Wave in NovemberTrump's nerves about a blue wave come November were clear to see during his address. Besides his declaration that America was doomed without him, the president turned heads when he seemed to offer voters a bribe to vote Republican. 

During his speech, Trump promised a $5,000 payment to every adult if the Republican Party wins both the House of Representatives and Senate on November 3.

"Because of our tremendous economic success, like in history, we've never had anything like what's happening, but because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000," he teased. "If the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000. 

"It will be called the Trump dividend."'We Don't Have Surpluses to Give Away'However, the "Trump dividend" left members of his own party divided – especially over how to fulfill the promise. With approximately 268 million adult Americans, the policy would cost the U.S. government $1.3trillion, immediately sparking inflation fears.

Such a deal could be considered illegal, with a punishment of up to a year in prison. Marc Goldwein, senior policy director at the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a think tank in Washington, said Trump has no authority to send money to Americans without approval from Congress.

Goldwein added that dividends are something that companies pay when there's a surplus, but the U.S. is running $2trillion in annual deficits and has $40trillion in debt.

"The idea that we've had fiscal success is backwards and bordering on laughable," he said. "We don't have surpluses to give away."
news.summary: The president took the podium at night one of the GOP's new midterm convention, trying to convince voters to keep Republicans in control of Congress.

news.title: Republican sounds alarm on rising Dem star: 'This guy’s going to be a problem'
news.text: DALLAS — There’s a rising star in the Democratic Party that is generating buzz for a possible presidential run, but one Republican argues he’s the only thing standing in the way of a future "DSA candidate" in 2028. Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., is running to unseat Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., in one of the most closely watched contests of this midterm election cycle. Ossoff has sought to nationalize their battle, focusing more on President Donald Trump and leaning into viral clips on social media to sell his message. But Collins told Fox News Digital during the GOP’s midterm convention that Ossoff’s intentions extended beyond a second term representing the Peach State. Instead, Collins charged that Ossoff is eyeing the White House and using this cycle as a springboard to get there. TRUMP-BACKED CANDIDATE SURVIVES GRUELING RUNOFF, ADVANCES TO HIGH-STAKES SENATE RACE "This guy is nothing but a trust fund kid who's never had a real job in his life," Collins said. "And at the end of the day, and I think the whole puzzle has been put together now, you can put the pieces of this thing so easy." "He caters to that far-left base, and at the end of the day, we've got to stop him in Georgia," he continued. "If we don't stop him in Georgia, this guy's going to be a problem for the entire country in 2028." Those puzzle pieces were scattered throughout his voting record, which Collins said aligned over 90% of the time with Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., through his support of progressives, like former Maine Senate Democratic nominee Graham Platner and Michigan Senate Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, and because the bulk of his campaign donations are from out-of-state. 'JESUS WAS A RADICAL': PROGRESSIVES INVOKE CHRIST TO SELL LEFT-WING AGENDA ON CAMPAIGN TRAIL Collins contended that the final piece was when the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) opened their first permanent field office in Atlanta last month. The organization has not endorsed Ossoff. "That just tells you, yes, Jon Ossoff is really running for president," Collins said. "He's going to be the DSA candidate. He uses Georgia as a platform to raise money." Ossoff’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment. OBAMA STRATEGIST TURNS ON RISING DEM STAR OVER VIRAL TRUMP ATTACK: 'GRATUITOUS AND UNNECESSARY' He has previously thrown cold water on the notion that he was chasing the White House and told MSNOW last month, "I have zero interest in running for president in 2028, and, frankly, zero interest in the 2028 fantasy football right now." The first-term senator is considered one of the most vulnerable incumbents on the Democrats’ Senate map this cycle, running in a state that Trump won in 2024 over former Vice President Kamala Harris by nearly three points. Still, he has gained national attention over the summer for his speeches on the campaign trail, particularly when he needled Trump in a viral social media clip bringing into question his relationship with his executive assistant, Natalie Harp. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "He doesn't want to do the job," Ossoff said. "He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar." That remark stoked a news cycle and earned him accolades from the likes of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., who noted that Ossoff was one of the top communicators on the trail when it came to targeting Trump.

news.title: Here’s Proof That James Talarico’s Campaign Is in BIG Trouble
news.text:
Texas State Rep. James Talarico (D-50th District), the Democrat running for U.S. Senate, is in serious trouble, and he knows it. I’m sure he knows it, even if he doesn’t want us to know the truth. But trust me, he just handed Republicans the proof.

Talarico recently sat down with Fox News, where national correspondent Brooke Taylor read back a string of his greatest hits on gender and transgender issues and asked him to explain himself. What followed was one of the more obvious campaign-trail reversals in recent memory.

"I oppose trans athletes playing in girls sports if it endangers safety or fairness," Talarico said.

Boy, that qualifier is doing a lot of work, isn't it? To the modern Democrat Party, letting biological men compete against women is fairness, because to them, "trans women are women." Talarico didn't abandon his position. He just learned to hide it behind a loophole big enough to drive a campaign bus through.

"I oppose trans athletes playing in girls sports if it endangers safety or fairness."Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico is changing his tune on biological men in women's sports.Pressed by Fox News' @Brooketaylortv on where he stands, Talarico said he would oppose trans… pic.twitter.com/o7JdCirul2— Fox News (@FoxNews) September 9, 2026

His voting record tells the real story. Talarico opposed and voted against both SB14, which banned surgical mutilation of minors, and SB15, which banned men from competing on women's sports teams. At the time, he wasn't dancing around a qualifier. Talarico said, "Some things are more important than perfectly fair competition in sports."

Recommended: Mark Kelly Actually Expects Us to Believe This Story?

He's also on record claiming there are "six" biological sexes and declaring that "God is nonbinary." These weren't offhand comments. For years, gender ideology seemed to define Talarico more than any other issue he touched.

So what changed? Nothing, really. Nobody believes Talarico had some late-in-life epiphany about girls' sports that just happened to present itself while he's running a statewide campaign in the red state of Texas. There's one logical explanation: his internal polling is telling him his record on trans issues is killing him with Texas voters. The GOP has been hammering him on it, and judging by this sudden, clumsy pivot, the attacks are landing.

Every election cycle, Democrats run the same play. As the general election approaches, they start pretending to be reasonable moderates. The problem is they govern like radical leftists the moment they're sworn in.

Remember how Kamala Harris tried to claim "no tax on tips" as her own in 2024, even though Donald Trump had the idea first? Or how Barack Obama sold himself as a uniter who'd work across the aisle? Heck, even Joe Biden ran in 2020 as the safe, moderate, "electable" alternative to the rest of the Democrat field, and he ultimately governed further to the left than Obama. It's the same con, over and over.

There's no other explanation for a candidate this deep into an ideological commitment suddenly discovering nuance three weeks before an election. If Talarico actually wins that Senate seat, he'll be voting with his party 100% of the time on these issues, because that's what Democrats do. But now he’s expecting us to believe that after years of being a radical on trans ideology, he’s suddenly changed his views. It’s a pivot that only a fool would believe to be true.

That's the proof his campaign is running scared. So ignore the polls showing him ahead. If he really believed that he was ahead, he wouldn't be flip-flopping on this now.

news.title: WSJ editor frets over 'scores of empty seats' at Trump speech
news.text:
On Thursday, following President Donald Trump’s speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas the previous evening, an editor at the Wall Street Journal was left worrying over the fact that there were “scores of empty seats.” As the Journal’s Damian Paletta wrote, “If Trump can’t fill a Dallas arena, can he turn out a November vote?”

“There were scores of empty seats in the upper tiers of the American Airlines Center for President Trump’s keynote address at the Republican convention,” noted Paletta. “And there were plenty of empty seats in the lower sections too. It was a five-hour drumroll of speakers leading up to the president’s remarks, but those seats never filled. The floor of the arena was rocking. That, in essence, represents his base of supporters. But those upper tiers and some of the other sections represent the difference makers in November. And they didn’t show up.”

This is the perfect “nutshell” explanation for the uphill battle Trump and Republicans face heading into the midterms. According to Paletta, “They need to, more than metaphorically, fill those seats. ‘Pretend I’m on the ballot,’ Trump told the arena during his speech, acknowledging that midterm elections can prove difficult for the party that controls the White House.” In Paletta’s assessment, Trump’s speech had lots of energy and “laugh lines,” but wondered, "Can that be enough?” Trump may not think so, because as Paletta notes, he promised every American adult $5000 if Republicans stay in power. 

But this “bribe,” as many are characterizing it, seems unlikely to turn a tide that is already decidedly against the Republicans. Trump’s historic unpopularity has many forecasting that the Democrats will win a majority in the House and maybe even the Senate, but as many conservatives have worried, the president seems strangely unconcerned. He was already dragging Republicans down due to his spiraling war with Iran and its resulting economic consequences, and has recently made a number of unpopular moves, like starting a trade war with Canada. This has resulted in a flurry of abysmal polls for the GOP, which have shown that many of the key voting blocs that carried Trump to office in 2024 – like independents, blue-collar workers, and the “reluctant right” who voted against Kamala Harris – have turned against Republicans. Now, polling shows that Democrats outpace Republicans in terms of midterm enthusiasm.

What’s more, Trump has sown division within his own party by endorsing scandal-plagued candidates like Ken Paxton in Texas, which many Republicans worry has cost them what was previously considered a safely red state. Trump has also been hesitant to open the $400 million war chest accumulated by his Super PAC MAGA Inc., and has repeatedly criticized his own party for its inability to pass his much-demanded voter ID law. According to Paletta, this tension within the GOP was evidenced by “the crowd’s awkward booing of Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD) halfway through Trump’s speech.”
news.summary:

news.text:
This is a solemn American moment — marking one day from our 25th remembrance of the 9/11 attacks and one year from the assassination of Charlie Kirk — so it’s fair to ask ourselves: What was the meaning of Donald Trump’s stemwinder last night in Dallas?

Trump was there to headline Day One of a unique two-day midterm convention, there in an effort to defy the history of the party in power nearly always getting thumped in the midterm elections.

But I think Trump was also there, whether knowingly or not, to defend the country he loves against the two anti-Western, anti-American forces that were responsible for those two awful aforementioned events: leftism and Islamism.

Oh, sure, Trump was promoting himself and his fellow Republicans last night as only Trump can. As I mentioned yesterday, he’s the animating force in the Republican Party, an animating force unlike any in its history or in our nation’s history. “Smoke ’em if you’ve got ’em,” we used to say in the military. Similarly, with Trump: Enjoy him while you’ve got him because his like will not pass this way again.

Last night’s warm-up act was one Republican speaker after another, and the recurring theme was “Common Sense vs. Crazy.” That’s a clever contrast between the Republicans and the Democrats, and we can expect to see it hammered home between now and November 3.

As for the 80-year-old president, he weaved away for nearly two hours, steering off script and then ultimately returning to it, tirelessly promoting his administration’s achievements and relentlessly attacking the Democrats.

Trump didn’t shy away from his ability to mobilize not only the Republican base but the Democrat base. In fact, he stressed it. “I’m asking you,” he yelled, “to pretend that I’m on the ballot. I’m on the ballot. I’m on the ballot. Just one more time.”

He added, “We have a very short period of time. And we really have 35 races. They all count, but we have 35 races that are, I guess you’d call swings, right?”

Republican strategist Reince Priebus said it felt “just like a presidential nominating convention,” but he also called this “a mobilization rather than a coronation.” Priebus said that if you move a thousand people in 20 different districts, that’s enough to alter the course of the election, and the course of history.

Trump went on to say that he’s going to campaign in every one of those 35 important races, and in some cases more than once. So by the time November 3 rolls around, the American electorate — both those who love Trump and those who loathe him — will know that this midterm election is a referendum on Trump.

The president’s best turn of phrase was toward the end, when he said, “On election night, we’re going to prove that America does not belong to the those who hate it; America belongs to those who love it.” That, too, will be seen and heard a lot between now and November.

But everyone knew, as soon as they heard him say it, what last night’s big buzz would be about:

I can make this promise to you, and here is my promise: If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them ... because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000 — very much like a successful company will do a cash distribution to its shareholders.

It was a brilliant promise, a check for $5,000 — and only spendable in America, and only payable if the Republicans hold both houses.

I have no doubt that the Democrats are already pulling together their best legal minds to argue that what he’s proposing is somehow illegal or unconstitutional, that it constitutes a bribe, an attempt to buy votes. To this I would ask: What do they think ObamaCare was?

The difference here, though, is that Trump’s transfer payment would go from the U.S. Treasury to all adult Americans, whereas Barack Obama’s transfer payment simply robbed a bunch of Peters to pay a bunch of Pauls.

Besides, what’s a measly $1.3 trillion to a fisc that’s already $40 trillion in arrears? I mean, we’ve got a country to save.

And double besides, if the legality of the “Trump Dividend” check were to somehow be fast-tracked to the Supreme Court before November 3, it seems to me that all Trump’s legal team would need to do is tell John Roberts ... that it’s a tax.

Trump’s backdrop was brilliant, too: all women, and all different colors. Because it’s women who typically side disproportionately with the Democrats on Election Day, and women who will thus decide whether Trump and his fellow Republicans pop the champagne corks on November 3, or gird themselves for articles of impeachment and endless investigations beginning on January 3, as soon as a new Democrat-controlled Congress is sworn in.

Trump also singled out the “fake news” for opprobrium, pausing on occasion to point them out way in the back, then marveling at the jam-packed venue, and then predicting that they’d find a few empty seats and write that there was no one there. And sure enough: “If Trump Can’t Fill a Dallas Arena, Can He Turn Out a November Vote?”

That was the headline of a Wall Street Journal piece, and it accompanied a deeply dishonest image of a sparsely populated arena. But the image wasn’t taken when Trump was speaking. How do I know it wasn’t taken when Trump was speaking, even if he’s too small to identify in the image? Because Trump’s backdrop for the entire speech was, as I noted above, a bunch of smiling and cheering women directly behind him.

Sadly, that’s the sort of reporting we can expect to see between now and November.

Toward the end of his speech, Trump paid tribute to his fallen friend and Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk, and to his wife, Erika, who was in attendance last night. Kirk was a champion of the free speech that Trump exercised last night, and he went out of his way to be courteous and respectful to his critics. Those who say Charlie Kirk was a hater are themselves haters. Either that, or they’re simply misinformed about who Kirk was and what he stood for.

I suspect there’ll be a more significant tribute to Charlie Kirk tonight, and that’s entirely fitting. Think about it: Did anyone work harder than him to promote and defend Christian and American principles, and to warn against the evils of leftism and the encroachment of Islam on Western Civilization? And did anyone besides Donald Trump himself work harder to ensure Trump’s victory over Kamala Harris in 2024?

There are now just 54 days until Election Day. Between now and then, make sure everyone you know knows Trump is on the ballot — and so is that $5,000 Trump Dividend check.

news.text:
Conservative Sarah Matthews went from serving as deputy press secretary in the first Trump administration to becoming a full-fledged Never Trumper and giving Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris an enthusiastic endorsement in 2024. This week, Matthews has a lot to say about Trump's social media rants, arguing that the type of content he posts shows the severity of his mental decline.

The Daily Beast's Ewan Palmer notes, "A former close aide to President Donald Trump has said the 80-year-old's unhinged Truth Social posts show he is losing touch with reality. Sarah Matthews, a White House deputy press secretary during Trump's first term, suggested that it is not only the sheer amount of AI-generated slop the president shares online that is worrying, but also, the sort of content he posts. This includes a particularly frantic posting spree on Sunday, when Trump shared dozens of deranged Truth Social updates, including one showing him with an army of robots launching a nuclear war on Earth from outer space, and another image of him threatening to beat Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney with a hockey stick."

During his first presidency, Trump did a lot of ranting on X (Twitter at the time). But according to Matthews, his social media posts are much worse now.

Matthews told the New York Times, "He floods the zone with so much of it that we've become numb to just how bizarre it is. An 80-year-old president is spending a ridiculous amount of time consuming and reposting endless AI fan fiction portraying him as the biggest, strongest, and most important person alive. It feels like we're genuinely watching his brain rot in real time."

Palmer points out that Trump's posts often "promote how he portrays himself in his head or how he wants to be seen" — for example, an "AI-generated image showing the U.S. military attacking Iran's oil hub of Kharg Island" as well as an image of "Trump smashing a chunk of land depicting Iran with a comically large hammer bearing the American flag on its head."

"It is not just Matthews — who resigned from the White House in the wake of the January 6 attack in 2021 and has since turned into a vocal Trump critic — who has expressed concerns about the president's social media addiction," Palmer observes. "There have been multiple demands to remove Trump from office via the 25th Amendment over suggestions that his Truth Social activity shows he is unfit for office. Democratic Rep. Chellie Pingree of Maine made such a call while sharing a video showing a stream of worrying content from Trump's Truth Social account on Sunday."

Pingree, in a September 6 post on X, wrote, "This is truly unhinged behavior from the president of the United States. And I don't want to hear 'oh, it's just Trump being Trump' or that he's 'trolling.' Enough. None of this is normal or okay. Republicans cannot keep shrugging this off. Congress, the Cabinet, and everyone around him has a responsibility to stop enabling this dangerous behavior and start asking whether he is fit to hold this office."
